```{=html}
<details class="x6-qa"><summary>Prairie City's council (fictional) weighs a heat-pump program. Which of its questions can the energy model answer by itself?</summary><ul><li><b>How much the winter evening peak changes if 2,000 homes switch.</b> Yes: given stated assumptions about the homes, an energy model computes the change in the peak.</li><li><b>Why renters rarely sign up.</b> No: reasons come from people, and interviews are one way to ask them.</li><li><b>Which program design residents would choose.</b> No: preferences come from people, and a choice experiment is one way to measure them.</li></ul></details><p class="lx-eyebrow">Six methods, what each asks, the data it needs and what it can tell a modeler</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table x6-fbt"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Method</th><th scope="col">Asks</th><th scope="col">Data</th><th scope="col">Gives a model</th><th scope="col">Cannot tell</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Survey</td><td>How many, how much, how often, across a population.</td><td>A questionnaire answered by a sample chosen to represent a population.</td><td>Estimated shares by household group, such as who has a heat pump.</td><td>People's reasons, in depth.</td></tr><tr><td>Interview</td><td>Why and how, in people's own words.</td><td>Open conversations with a few chosen people, recorded and transcribed.</td><td>Reasons, barriers and assumptions worth testing, including ones a model leaves out.</td><td>How common each view is across a city.</td></tr><tr><td>Choice experiment</td><td>Which trade-offs people accept.</td><td>Repeated choices between offers whose features vary, made by a sample of people.</td><td>Each feature's weight, such as bill saving against control, for estimating how many take up an offer.</td><td>Real behavior: the choices are stated, not observed.</td></tr><tr><td>Ethnography</td><td>How people live with energy, day to day.</td><td>Long observation and conversation in homes or communities.</td><td>Routines a model's behavior rules should reflect, such as how heating is really used.</td><td>Numbers that hold for a whole city.</td></tr><tr><td>Document-based policy analysis</td><td>How rules came about, and who shaped them.</td><td>Laws, rulings, official case records and the documents parties submitted, read and compared over time.</td><td>The rules and limits a model must respect, and which could change.</td><td>Everyday experience the records miss, especially of people who left no record.</td></tr><tr><td>Participatory mapping</td><td>Which places matter to people, and why.</td><td>Residents mark places on maps, in workshops or online.</td><td>Map layers used to compare possible locations, to exclude or weigh, as in lesson A19.</td><td>How the whole population feels, when few take part.</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="lx-eyebrow">Six questions and the method that fits each best, with the reason</p><ul><li>To target the program: what share of each income group had trouble paying an energy bill last year?<br>Survey: a questionnaire to a sample chosen to represent all households estimates shares by group; who responds affects how reliable they are.</li><li>Why do landlords turn down a free heat-pump upgrade for their rental homes?<br>Interviews: open questions to a few landlords bring out reasons no one listed in advance.</li><li>How much bill saving would a household trade for letting the utility adjust its heat pump at the peak?<br>Choice experiment: people pick between offers that vary saving and control, revealing the trade-off they accept.</li><li>How do families live with a new heat pump through a winter, and what does comfort mean to them?<br>Ethnography: time spent with households shows routines people may not report in a survey.</li><li>How did the state's rules for utility heat-pump rebates come about over ten years, and who argued for what?<br>Document-based policy analysis: statutes, rulings and submitted documents read and compared over the decade.</li><li>Which streets and blocks do residents say the program should reach first, and why?<br>Participatory mapping: residents mark the places that matter, which planners can turn into map layers.</li></ul><p class="lx-eyebrow">Which methods involve people as participants</p><ul><li><b>Survey.</b> People take part: ask the ethics board first what review and consent apply; it also decides whether any requirement can be relaxed.</li><li><b>Interview.</b> People take part: ask the ethics board first what review and consent apply; it also decides whether any requirement can be relaxed.</li><li><b>Choice experiment.</b> People take part: ask the ethics board first what review and consent apply; it also decides whether any requirement can be relaxed.</li><li><b>Ethnography.</b> People take part: ask the ethics board first what review and consent apply; it also decides whether any requirement can be relaxed.</li><li><b>Document-based policy analysis.</b> Mostly documents; once officials are interviewed, or identifiable personal records are used, ask the ethics board too.</li><li><b>Participatory mapping.</b> People take part: ask the ethics board first what review and consent apply; it also decides whether any requirement can be relaxed.</li></ul><details class="x6-qa"><summary>A survey finds that homes in the heat-pump program use less energy than homes outside it. Does that show the program cut their use?</summary><ul><li><b>Yes: the difference is the effect.</b> Not by itself: homes that joined may have used less before the program (selection).</li><li><b>Not by itself: the homes that joined may differ.</b> Right: joiners may differ before the program; lesson M14's methods build a fair comparison.</li><li><b>No: surveys cannot measure energy use.</b> No: a survey can record use or bills; the trouble is the comparison, not the survey.</li></ul></details><p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you match the questions to methods, open each method, mark which involve people and test one survey result.</p>
```

## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="x06-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- x06-ideas:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<dl class="lx-ideas"><dt>Different questions</dt><dd>Each method answers its own kind of question: how many, why, which trade-off, how people live, how rules came about, which places matter.</dd><dt>For a modeler</dt><dd>Findings become inputs, household groups, behavior rules, constraints, map layers or scenarios.</dd><dt>Ethics board first</dt><dd>Before research with people, or with identifiable records about them, ask the institution's ethics board what review and consent apply; it also decides whether any requirement can be relaxed.</dd><dt>Not causal by itself</dt><dd>A difference between joiners and others does not, by itself, establish the program's effect; a fair comparison is a design choice of its own.</dd><dt>Neutral</dt><dd>No method is ranked above another here: each is the right tool for some questions and the wrong one for others.</dd></dl>
<!-- x06-ideas:end -->
</div>
</div>
<!-- x06-stop:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-card xs-stop" id="x06-stop"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Where we stop</p><h3>This side topic stops at choosing a method</h3><p class="xs-stop-lede">Social-science methods enter the course as what each can tell a modeler and how to work with the people who use them; training in a method is beyond it.</p><div class="xs-stop-cols"><div><h4 class="xs-h">This side topic covers</h4><ul><li>What six methods answer, the data each needs and what each cannot tell.</li><li>Why research with people starts with the ethics board, which decides what review and consent apply.</li><li>How findings become a model's inputs, groups, layers or scenarios.</li></ul></div><div><h4 class="xs-h">Left to specialists</h4><ul><li>Training in any method: sampling, interview guides, experimental design, coding.</li><li>Designing questionnaires, choice sets or mapping workshops.</li><li>Fieldwork itself.</li></ul></div></div><h4 class="xs-h">Read next, three rungs</h4><ol class="xs-ladder"><li><b>Start here.</b> How energy social scientists choose and combine methods, with codes of practice for each family (open access). <span class="xs-src"><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.erss.2018.07.007">Sovacool, Axsen and Sorrell (2018), Promoting novelty, rigor, and style in energy social science</a>, published 3 October 2018</span></li><li><b>Go further.</b> An introductory social-science research-methods textbook, for how each method is designed and judged. <span class="xs-src">Bryman, Social Research Methods (Oxford University Press), cited by name, any recent edition</span></li><li><b>Go deep.</b> The rules for research with people on DOE-supported projects, including who decides on review and on exemptions; your university's ethics board publishes its own guide. <span class="xs-src"><a href="https://www.energy.gov/documents/doe-o-443-1-dprotection-human-research-subjects2026-07-23pdf">U.S. Department of Energy, Order 443.1D, Protection of Human Research Subjects</a>, approved 5 August 2026</span></li></ol></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Researcher</span>Working with social scientists</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li><b>Start together.</b> Bring a social scientist in while the question is being framed, not after the model is built.</li>
<li><b>Agree what the model needs.</b> Shares by group, weights, routines, rules or map layers, each with its units, date and population.</li>
<li><b>Ask the ethics board first.</b> It decides what review and consent the plan needs, and whether any requirement can be relaxed, before data are collected; lesson R9 shows how.</li>
<li><b>Close the loop.</b> Tell participants what was found and how their answers were used.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<!-- x06-check:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="x06-myth"><div class="lx-qq" data-id="volunteers" data-answer="myth"><p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “An online poll of 50 volunteers shows what share of a city's households struggle with their energy bills.”</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Volunteers choose themselves; a share for the whole city needs a sample drawn to represent it, as large surveys such as EIA's do.</p></details></div></div><div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="x06"><div class="lx-qq" data-id="count" data-answer="a"><p class="lx-qtext">A modeler needs to know how many of a city's homes have a heat pump today, by income group. Which method fits best?</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">A survey of a representative sample</li><li data-value="b">Ethnography in a few homes</li><li data-value="c">Interviews with installers</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>A survey: a representative sample estimates shares or numbers by group, and who responds affects how reliable they are; ethnography and interviews explain how and why.</p></details></div></div>
<!-- x06-check:end -->
```
